content:
At a Lean event in Paris last week I chatted with someone who is interested in Lean, and had a background in using Isabelle, and expressed sadness that Lean does not have the kind of explicitly structured, nicely edited, easy to read, robust to change Isar-style proofs. That, as well as Larry Paulson's “Why not Lean” blog post (which, I learned, is not criticizing Lean itself) made me think about Isar, and whether I miss it in Lean.

For my PhD I formalized something in Isabelle, and I took pride in writing a proof document that reads well. I may have explored my proofs in the apply-script style (i.e. a tactic proof), but cleaned it up to be structured, to call out assumptions and goals, and to make the dependencies between the forward steps explicit. I even showed that off in my thesis and wrote a section on the aesthetics of a formal proof:

Later in my life, in Philadelphia, I worked on a project that used what is now called Rocq, and I remember that I did feel disappointment from not having Isar-style proofs. Tactics felt arcane, pedestrian, imperative. Back then, using bullets to have indentation match code structure was just about cutting edge, and my feeble asks for more structure at the Rocq issue tracker did not make a big difference. But in the end I used what was there and I was fine with it.

Fast forward to my time using Lean. Lean does not provide much more structure than what Rocq offered back then. Bullets and (at least!) named cases. I still fondly remember my carefully written Isar proofs, but do I really miss them while working with Lean? Not so much actually. Certainly not enough to fix it, which I could. And not because I’m working at the FRO – Lean is such an extensible system, that anyone out there who is bothered enough by the lack of Isar-style proofs in Lean could create that!

Luckily (or not depending how you think about GenAI), these days such existential statements can be made much more constructively: Over the weekend, in maybe 4 or 5 half-hour sessions, I had an LLM create a proof of concept Isar library for lean. It doesn’t cover everything Isar does, but already plenty of it, probably close to the proverbial 80% – including important ideas such as that local facts are only visible to the proof steps that are explicitly using them. It even comes with a custom InfoView view into the Isar state…

You can play around with it, get it from https://github.com/nomeata/lean-lisar. But do not bother reporting bugs for this PoC, as this is not a product; for that it would need a human maintainer and a more careful design. But it could well be the starting point for someone who wants to create a usable Isar-for-Lean library. And I think it proves that there is nothing fundamental preventing Lean users from having an Isar-like experience. It doesn’t even have to be built in!

So circling back to my original question: Why there is no Isar in Lean, and why are there nevertheless so many Lean users mostly happy with its tactic language? It cannot be because it’s not possible, as just demonstrated.

  • So it _could_ be because too few people know about the pleasures of Isar, and structured proofs will appear in due time once someone is simultaneously bothered by the lack of it and inspired to do the necessary bits of meta programming.
  • Or it just happens that the bit of structure lean has (bullets and case always; have, show and calc when you want them) is simply good enough.

In either case, at least for me the lack of Isar is no longer a “why not Lean”.

(All thoughts in this post are my own.)

Joachim Breitner said:

Why there is no Isar in Lean, and why are there nevertheless so many Lean users mostly happy with its tactic language?

Well I'll give you my own thoughts. I have honestly never understood anything about this discussion of ITP proof style. I don't even understand what you are trying to demonstrate by this page from your thesis. You just do a long calculation, and each line is justified by "this is trivial for anyone who knows what is going on". You then show some Isabelle code where the proofs are the same. I genuinely do not understand the point you are making. 95% of proofs in mathlib are completely trivial to any mathematician who knows the theory and surely nobody in their right mind would want to read them. What point am I missing here? Are you suggesting that it would be better to have a human-readable proof of x+y=y+x for some reason? Who is your audience who you are imaginging is reading these proofs? I am totally confused.

In FLT I am writing LaTeX precisely to give humans something to read. Machines can read the Lean proofs.

I guess when writing calc blocks, it's nice to have the also have functionality? I usually "hack" this behavior by writing 

have := calc X = Y := by sorry
            _ = Z := by sorry

and then you can add whatever lines you want to the calc block and have Lean compile and respond to you.

I once wrote some Lean proofs about topological modules for which I could find no reference in the literature, and when I PRed them to mathlib I simply added a boatload of comments so that humans could read them easily without having to read any of the code. Isn't this better than Isar because then any human could read it, not just humans who know something about Isabelle code.

Presumably the idea is that you wouldn't need to spend extra lines writing comments, if the formal code reads close to human? (I'm personally ok with people needing to learn to read Lean, it's really not all that hard... We learned LaTeX, and this is not much harder.)

I think your “need for the boatload of comments” show why some people are fond of Isar, where

  • such comments are less needed, because one can more likely follow the formal proof and
  • they are not comments, but part of the formal proof, so they don't got out of sync.

For the 95% of proofs that nobody needs to read anyways, the discussion is pointless indeed. This is, if anything, about the 5% of proofs where you want to convey a nice idea.

OK if the point being made is "there is an ITP tactic language which is human-readable but Lean's is not" then my response would be that (a) I don't actually believe that there is an ITP tactic language which is human-readable, I believe that what is really going on is that people who use ITP tactic languages get good at reading them and then start to think that they're easy to read and (b) I claim that Lean is easy to read if you have it up and running in a live Lean session with an infoview, or have access to the infoview because of Verso, and if you're not reading Lean in that context then I would question whether you're doing the right thing.

How about you make Lean tactic proofs more readable by writing show [write the goal here] on every other line of a tactic proof? How is that any different to Isar? That won't get out of sync, it would make it easier to follow the formal proof if you were foolish enough to be reading it on paper -- does that solve all the problems? I am honestly just trying to understand the point here. For years I have been bewildered by this discussion and perhaps now is the time to try and understand what I am missing.

I think that my comment approach, which explains what each tactic application is doing rather than showing the before/after state, is much more readable then show [write the goal here]. Indeed in your example, many of your comments explaining how to get from each line to the next (e.g. "by the induction hypothesis") seem to be missing in the Isar code (or have become simp). So in fact the best stuff is gone.

Why there is no Isar in Lean, and why are there nevertheless so many Lean users mostly happy with its tactic language?

You can write more readable proofs in vanilla Lean with no extra notation, but spamming tactics and easier, and that's what people do. In contrast, Isar forces you to write clean proof because you can't just rw it into an unreadable mess.

A conjecture about what is going on: I think that mathematicians and computer scientists are interested in different kinds of proofs, and/or have different relationships with proofs. Thinking about it, I think that the only people I've ever spoken to about this Isar business are computer scientists (I have been asked several times about proof readability by computer scientists and have always been confused). I think that as a mathematician I value higher order ideas far more than technical details when it comes to explainability; in mathematics we have this attitude that many things are trivial and just boring and technical, so we leave many of them to the reader in our own writings. I guess you can't program like that! I am more interested in projects like the Massot/Miller unformalization project, which translates things into English which a mathematician can certainly read. So perhaps the value of this project is in CS applications? What do the CSLib people think I wonder?

I'm sorry for my aggressive-sounding posts -- they were not supposed to be aggressive. They come from a genuine confusion which I think simply means that I'm not the target audience for projects like this.

Kevin Buzzard said:

I am more interested in projects like the Massot/Miller unformalization project, which translates things into English which a mathematician can certainly read.

This raises a question: why writing the same thing in English instead of code would make it more readable? Especially if details are trivial and you don't need to read them at all?

And if English is readable because it says a completely different thing (indeed, in prose people usually state things instead describing a sequence of transformations of the proof goal), then why do we write code in such a cryptic way?

Sometimes the English is very important because the idea of the proof is impossible to write in Lean, since technically it doesn't work, but it is still where almost everything happens. Of course in this situation one should write explicitly something like "this is the idea, but since our spaces are only almost foobar we cannot literally follow it".

suhr said:

This raises a question: why writing the same thing in English instead of code would make it more readable?

Is the point of Isar "we want to make this code more readable for people who understand Isabelle already" or "we want to make this code more readable for all of humanity"? If the point is being able to reach all of humanity then I would say that many mathematicians (especially those of my age) find all code (including python code) intimidating, and find code written in any ITP language at all even more intimidating, but find English extremely readable, even if it says things like "the remaining 37 cases are left to the reader" -- this is the way we communicate. We like to get ideas across by explaining high-level concepts, not nitty-gritty boring details. This is why I am conjecturing that the question of more or less readable computer code might be something has more meaning or value for those who already are good at writing computer code, or at least for those who are not intimidated by it.

I really don't want to derail this conversation any more so I will shut up now. Joachim's question is "what do you think of my Isar thing" and I think it would be much more valuable to talk about that than for me to continue demonstrating why I have a poor understanding of this area of research.

My point is mostly: one can have Isar in Lean, if one wants. So the lack of Isar in Lean is not a fundamental deficiency, merely a sign that there is just not a strong enough demand, for whatever reasons (well exemplified by your comments :-))

Kevin Buzzard schrieb:

95% of proofs in mathlib are completely trivial to any mathematician who knows the theory and surely nobody in their right mind would want to read them.

to any mathematician who knows the theory carries a lot of weight here.
In my experience to a mathematician nearly everything is trivial exactly from the point where he has understood it (which can be frustrating to anyone not having understood it).

It sucks that Mathlib isn't a good learning resource.

I am more interested in projects like the Massot/Miller unformalization project, which translates things into English which a mathematician can certainly read.

I also find this project highly interesting, but unfortunately it still requires the proofs to be written in a certain style to work well. And if i remember correctly it just can't generate then and moreover ... ultimately-style chains because this info just isn't there in the Lean source. If we had some way to communicate which lines are needed for what these projects would likely be much more useful.

Kevin Buzzard said:

I am more interested in projects like the Massot/Miller unformalization project, which translates things into English which a mathematician can certainly read. So perhaps the value of this project is in CS applications? What do the CSLib people think I wonder?

I find this work very interesting. Like many proof assistant users, I have a bit of a mixed background in math and CS. I do think there are some hard to pin down differences in how each use proof assistants, but I find this sort of experimentation generally applicable to readability and usability. I tend to agree with you though that this is most helpful to those who are already proof assistant users or at least done some programming. It has a different scope in my view than projects that aim for bridging the gap to English pen and paper math.

I think in general that the idea of more structured metadata and organization of the proof state is very interesting for formal proof ergonomics. For instance, the "fact stack" mirrors certain ways I naturally structure proofs, especially when automation is involved and I want a tightly controlled local context. An idea I've had myself is that this sort of metaprogramming could be used to put more structure to the idea of a proof having "side goals". If this is actually recorded as information attached to the goal, you could imagine automatically structuring the proof to keep the main argument in focus and delay side goals to the end for the purposes of presentation.

(And as a side note Joachim, thanks for the upfront and thoughtful AI disclosure!)

(And as a side note Joachim, thanks for the upfront and thoughtful Al disclosure!)

Thanks! I'll pass it on to Claude, it formulated that part, too ;-)

My view is that mathlib-style proofs use forward-reasoning at the file level and backward-reasoning at the lemma level. If the proof of a single lemma uses forward reasoning, it likely consists of a bunch of have statements, and it is often better to refactor them out into their own lemmas. This is how we end up with hundreds of thousands of lemmas in mathlib with < 5 line proofs.

Backwards reasoning cannot be factored out into its own lemmas, so the proof language should be optimized for backwards reasoning. Tactics are weird in that they are imperative whereas most mathematicians would think of proofs as declarative, but it makes sense to me that backwards reasoning is more imperative than forward reasoning.

With that said, this mainly applies to mathlib-style proofs, and there are legitimate reasons to prefer Isar style proofs. I think it is a great strength of Lean that if the language doesn't suit your use case, you can extend it with metaprogramming.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Thinking about it, I think that the only people I've ever spoken to about this Isar business are computer scientists (I have been asked several times about proof readability by computer scientists and have always been confused).

I have always thought that Isar proofs are more readable than Lean proofs. So unless you want to claim I'm not a mathematician, there are mathematicians who also think this.
I honestly don't know how to interpret the :pray: react in this context, to be honest.
"Thanks for pointing out that mathematicians exist who think that Isar proofs are more readable than Lean proofs, it seems like a reasonable thing to add to the conversation" was what I meant.

I've never used Isar, but I'd like to add one point: the first proof assistant I used was Rocq (because of an internship at Inria), and when I tried out Agda, it was a revelation and I started hating tactic proofs. These weren't proofs I showed to anyone, but I found the readability useful while writing the proof. Part of it may be due to inexperience, but in Rocq, I was always having trouble when I found out in the middle of the proof that I had to change something earlier, because of the mental effort to navigate proof states and figure out what to change in a tactic script to adapt it to a slightly changed hypothesis. I do really miss having some tactics in Agda, e.g., for deciding Presburger arithmetic (akin to Lean's omega and Rocq's lia), but I only want tactics which close the goal, not tactics which change the proof state and leave me chasing down what it looks like now. (But I also want more convenient ways to rewrite things, which is a bit hard to do in that style.)

Some scattered thoughts:

  • The "don't know Isar" for me holds for the infoview, but not for the proof script syntax.
  • As some people have mentioned already, I think the assessment here depends a lot on whether you assume reading the proof scripts in an IDE with an infoview or also (or just) as plaintext. (I consider both).
  • I think there is an somewhat orthogonal issue here, which is the (un)availibility of tactics representing mathematical ideas. If you have a proof that's something like measurability; positivity, then I would argue this is the part that gives the information, rather than recording the intermediate proof state. If the intermediate steps are just bookkeeping, including it might make it more readable as plaintext, but duplicate information if you're working with an infoview.
  • To me, Isar-style feels like a halfway house between plain Lean and Verbose Lean: Some more effort to write, but not necessarily nice to read for a non-Lean user.
  • I feel like the style encouraged by Isar is often argued against in Mathlib PRs. I think the intermediate-show solution could help with readability of proof scripts, but again, duplicates infoview-based information.
  • I think Isar proofs are slightly more readable then Lean-proofs in the examples I've seen, but plain Isabelle feels a lot less readable than either.

In short: I think the reason we don't have Lean-Isar is more of an accumulation of various small reasons, rather than 1 big reason.

My two cents:

  1. I don't find Isar much more readable than lean proofs written in an equally careful manner. I do find them more readable than whatever golfing mathlib does to proofs. Especially all those refine <?_, <?_,?_> like lines.
  2. CS is such a vast area that it is unlikely any two subfields have the same idea of what readable proofs look like. So asking opinions of CSLib people would get you drastically different responses @Kevin Buzzard. ITP use has a deep and rich history in specific niches of CS and has been virtually non-existent elsewhere.
  3. Personally I find that I like proofs that I can follow as a series of haves and lets which are sufficiently succinct that I can follow the flow of the proofs without looking into the details. Sometimes when I write a proof like this, I just need to read the last few lines and then figure out which haves I care about. Unfortunately this style gets labelled as being too LLM-like. This goes to show that readability is very subjective.

To me, Lean proofs (at least the ones I've been writing for real analysis) can be made readable by using intermediate have statements, not packing too many tactics per line, and avoiding term mode. So I personally don't feel a strong need for a different structure or syntax for the logical flow of proofs in Lean.

What makes Lean proofs look far from traditional paper proofs is the extra rigor around what mathematicians call "abuse of notation" on specific mathematical objects (beyond just the logic). For example, 0 in ℕ is not 0 in ℝ, and despite norm_cast/push_cast and the coercion infrastructure, the need for calling that injection explicitly can end up diluting proofs in Lean. I have never seen a math proof which needed to make that distinction explicit.

This isn't unique to type theory — I think technically it's true in ZFC too, math proofs just paper over it by convention. So if the goal is to make Lean proofs closer to informal ones, this technical layer needs to be hidden somehow, not just syntactically rephrased.

Are there attempts to solve this for math objects more generally somehow? Or is the best path just accumulating more domain-specific tactics like push_cast for particular abuses of notation as they come up? Even just calling the tactic technically distances the Lean proof from the paper proof.

Oh, and really cool prototype. Exposes new comers to ITP (like me) to ideas outside lean, and shows off the expressiveness of lean as an extensible language. As I heard it said "AI made prototypes free" and I am all for more prototypes :)

Rado Kirov said:

[...]>What makes Lean proofs look far from traditional paper proofs is the extra rigor around what mathematicians call "abuse of notation" on specific mathematical objects (beyond just the logic). For example, 0 in ℕ is not 0 in ℝ, and despite norm_cast/push_cast and the coercion infrastructure, the need for calling that injection explicitly can end up diluting proofs in Lean. I have never seen a math proof which needed to make that distinction explicit.

This isn't unique to type theory — I think technically it's true in ZFC too, math proofs just paper over it by convention. So if the goal is to make Lean proofs closer to informal ones, this technical layer needs to be hidden somehow, not just syntactically rephrased.

The main exception is when proving soundness of abuse of notation. E.g. cast distributivity theorems, categorical 'strictness' and 'coherence', and so on. But indeed these are hidden from view when they're not needed — which is most of the time, or else we'd be using different notation!

I like the idea of enabling "rify as needed" within a section scope, turning it off only when I need to lift a new operator into notation
hmm, is this what makes inheritance diamonds and defeq abuse more tempting?

The discussion here has focused on readability. For me, the main advantage of Isar however is maintainability. (I'm the sad person mentioned in Joachim's introduction ;). )

Isar gives you a nice structured way of baking into the code how facts and variable bindings come together. Practically this means that, if some definition change breaks a proof, it's usually trivial to fix it for an Isar proof. (Even if others have written it or years have passed!)

With longer Isabelle-apply-scripts on the other hand, it's perfectly possible that a proof breaks in quite non-local ways that are hard to understand and force you to cross-compare proof state sequences between versions or redo a whole block. People try to prevent the issue by splitting up proofs into a lot of small lemmas, but that spams the namespace (and the assumption lists of the sublemmas). I have the impression that similar things are going on in Lean, or at least, that the language makes it convenient to write proofs with such maintainability problems.

Isar makes it handy to control the context of proof steps and encourages it. That's why, although I do not love every design aspect of Isar and do not care so much about emulating math-paper proofs, I'd prefer Isar-style structured proofs over tactic sequences/trees any day.

Benjamin Bisping said:

People try to prevent the issue by splitting up proofs into a lot of small lemmas, but that spams the namespace (and the assumption lists of the sublemmas).

This sounds pretty much like what's happening in mathlib, although it's not necessarily a bad thing.

Rado Kirov said:

This isn't unique to type theory — I think technically it's true in ZFC too, math proofs just paper over it by convention.

This is not true. Set theory gives you greater flexibility than standard type theories with regards to treating things as literal subobjects. If you want to regard the natural numbers as literally being a specific subset of the complex numbers, you are free to do this, and indeed this is what is done in Metamath.

Interesting; how is that done? Do you have “proto-nats” that you use to bootstrap the definition of reals, and then define your working definition of nats as a subset of the reals? Or do you use a construction of the reals that is somehow so that nats are a subset of them?

Joachim Breitner said:

Interesting; how is that done? Do you have “proto-nats” that you use to bootstrap the definition of reals, and then define your working definition of nats as a subset of the reals?

I believe this is basically it, yes. Metamath uses ω\omegaω for the von Neumann ordinal and N\mathbb{N}N for the set of positive integers as a subset of the complex numbers.
This is even roughly how they describe it too.
